Let me analyze these teaching examples carefully to identify systematic errors in the model forecasts compared to true outcomes, and how sentiment history might help correct them.

## Example 1: Date=2024-08-16

History is around 71-72 range, slightly declining from peak
Model forecasts are still around 72.5-73.7 on day 1, then slowly decline to 70.5 by day 7
True outcomes: 72.52, 73.14, 73.07, 72.14, 71.57, 71.13, 70.49, 71.49, 70.77, 71.06, 70.30, 70.43, 68.16, 67.00, 66.20, 66.50, 66.52, 64.92, 66.40, 65.45, 64.99, 63.21, 64.34, 63.70, 62.82, 63.39, 64.10, 63.87, 65.24, 66.52

Looking at the divergence:
- Day 1-3: Model is slightly too high (off by ~0.4-0.6)
- Day 4-7: Model overestimates by ~1-2 points initially, but catches up
- Day 8-12: Model is still ~0.3-0.6 too high
- Day 13+: Model is significantly too high until about day 16
- Days 17-20: Model forecasts are ~2-3 points too high
- Days 21-24: Model is ~1-2 points too high
- Days 25-27: Model is ~1 point too high
- Days 28-30: Model is ~1.5-2 points too high

Wait, let me look at this more carefully. The model forecasts on day 1 were 72.56, 73.34, 73.69...


The true outcomes begin at 72.52, 73.14, 73.07, showing a consistent 0.04-0.62 difference. As days progress, the divergence shifts from minor overestimates to more pronounced variations. By day 4-7, the model's predictions diverge more significantly, with differences ranging from 0.97 to 2.03 points
